videos.caption: A new catastrophe has hit Nepal mere weeks after a deadly flood which killed over a thousand people… this time claiming an entire mountain. Dramatic footage has emerged of the moment the mountainside collapsed along the Kali Gandaki River, with a large section breaking apart and sliding directly into the river. The incident comes just one month after the 26th August glacier-and-rock collapse in the Langatang region which triggered apocalyptic flooding, claiming the lives of more than 3,000 people and left thousands more missing. While happening in very close proximity to that disaster, this latest incident cannot automatically be described as having been caused by it. Scientists have, however, warned that warming temperatures, glacier retreat and thawing mountain permafrost are making the Himalayan slopes increasingly unstable.

Rescuers recovered four bodies and brought 10 people to safety before bad weather suspended operations on Monday, with 12 individuals still missing. Nepal’s youngest prime minister Balendra Shah told world leaders at the UN that Nepal’s latest flash floods that killed more than 1,400 people are a “close warning for humanity,” and that action is needed now. On Aug. 26, deadly flash floods caused by a glacial collapse struck Nepal, sweeping through villages along the Nepal-Tibet border, killing more than 1,494 people and leaving more than 6,150 people missing. On Thursday, Sept. 24, Shah addressed the UN General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City for the first time. “The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy; it was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?” Shah said. Shah recalled that UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of an impending climate disaster at the foot of Mount Everest nearly three years ago, and called out world leaders for failing to act despite local communities and scientists reporting the effects of climate change He said climate change, as seen in the floods, affected people across Nepal and Tibet and will affect everyone. “Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps on passports,” he said. Shah said that Nepal did not create the climate crisis, contributing less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, but is still paying a “colossal price.” According to Shah, Nepal would need to use 10% of its gross domestic product (GDP) to rebuild from the floods, adding that it cannot be constantly rebuilding. While Shah did not ask for financial aid, he told leaders that the Loss and Damage Fund, the Global Environment Facility and other financial mechanisms remain “grossly inadequate.” “Climate finance must not become another bureaucratic mess through which vulnerable countries spend years that they need help,” he said. “When the house is burning, we do not ask the family to complete 50 forms. We act.” Shah also called for cooperation between Nepal, India and China to improve climate resilience and disaster response across the Himalayas. #nepal #balendrashah #un #climate #fyp
